The chaotic nature of weather means that no conclusion about climate can ever be drawn from a single data point, hot or cold. The temperature of one place at one time is just weather, and says nothing about climate, much less climate change, much less global climate change.

But the earth has been around sooo long. Having great climate shifts, ice ages, etc. Even while humans existed. Did "global warming" cause the tropical oasis of Egypt to dry up? No. Things change. Believing the whole history of the world is summed up in the past 135 years of measurements is absurd

Climate absolutely changes over time naturally. However something that has changed is that this is the first time we're seeing rapid change in climate and having humans are contributing an enormous amount to an increasingly unnatural and powerful greenhouse effect. The thing that makes me concerned about climate change is that by the time you reach the point that your average Joe is saying holy shit - we need to do something now!! it's already far too late and probably has been for some years. It's like deciding to stop smoking once you already have cancer and emphysema.

And also something you may not realize is that though various greenhouse gases do dissipate naturally we're pumping them in far faster than they're dissipating. So it's not like we have, let's say, "100" units of unnatural gasses in the sky and we're more or less maintaining that same level so long as we don't radically increase our release of various greenhouse gases. Instead it's like we have 100 units this year, 110 next year, 120 the year after, and so on. And even that is understating the picture since our production of greenhouse gases, with CO2 being one of the most dangerous not because of its impact but because of how long it takes to dissipate, is increasing. So it's more like 100 units this year 110 next year, 125 the year after, 145 the following year, and so on.

Well, yeah, it seems to have been rather warm so far this summer in North Carolina, but that just offsets the previous two summers which were notably cool.
